Werkligâs web design for Finnish energy firm Voltcore pairs Store Norske Skandia and Skandia Mono across foggy snow ridges and grid hardware.

Recent findings suggest that A snow-packed ridge fades into pale winter fog across Voltcoreâs opening screen, pushing the white headline down into the lower-left corner. Up top, thereâs no clutter. Just a spaced VOLTCORE wordmark on the left and four tiny monospaced links (About, Services, Team, Contact) pinned to the right edge. Helsinki studio Werklig designed the identity and site for the Finnish energy company, which develops grid-balancing, baseload, and hybrid power assets across the Nordics. Featured on Fonts In Use, the web design runs on two siblings from Skriftkompani: Store Norske Skandia and Store Norske Skandia Mono. Scroll past that frosty hero and photography drops away, leaving three oversized charcoal paragraphs under a tiny About us tag to explain why Nordic grids need weather-independent power in dark winters.

Industry observers note that werklig gives each typeface a strict job, and it doesnât blur the line. Store Norske Skandia carries headlines and statements, while Store Norske Skandia Mono handles navigation, eyebrows, and captions with the crisp cadence of an engineering log. That split sharpens in the three-column What we do grid below. Three desaturated vertical photographs sit side by side: ribbed ceramic substation insulators against grey sky, a lattice transmission tower half-swallowed by mist, and an overhead power-line switch silhouetted against stark white. Beneath every frame sits an identical three-step stack â a mono tag for Balancing, Baseload, or Hybrid, a proportional subhead, and a tight monospaced caption. No rounded cards or drop shadows get in the way, so the web design reads cleanly on a single scan.

It has been revealed that near the bottom, winter returns up close. A wind-carved snowdrift curves across the contact band in blue-grey shadow, holding white display copy above a full-width hairline rule and [email protected]. Directly underneath, a pale-grey footer splits into four monospaced columns for Voltcore Oyâs phone line, Helsinki street address, Business ID 3638975-9, and a Back to top arrow. Itâs plain operational typography, right down to the registry number. Then the bottom strip snaps to pure white, stretching a monumental black VOLTCORE wordmark edge to edge. That final scale jump flips the compact header mark into a stark closing band for the web design.

What Science Reveals About Gratitude’s Impact on the Brain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health.
  • Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion.
  • Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health. But very little is known about what actually happens in our brain and body when we experience it.

Why does that matter? Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion. The goal of my research has been to lay the groundwork for understanding what happens in the brain when we feel grateful—and a picture of the grateful brain is now starting to emerge.

Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.

When I first embarked on the journey to study gratitude, I came across philosophical treatises and religious exhortations emphasizing the importance of gratitude, along with scientific studies suggesting that gratitude can improve your sleep, enhance your romantic relationships, protect you from illness, motivate you to exercise, and boost your happiness, among many other benefits.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, however, very little was known about what happens in our brains and bodies when we experience gratitude, which made it difficult to understand how gratitude actually works. Since I’m a neuroscientist, I zeroed in on the neurobiology of gratitude with a more specific question in mind: Can our brain activity reveal anything about how gratitude achieves its significant benefits?

Recent findings suggest that given the clear relationship between mental and physical health, I thought that understanding what happens in the brain when we feel gratitude could tell us more about the mind-body connection—namely, how feeling positive emotion can improve bodily functions. I also thought these results could help scientists design programs aimed at generating gratitude by helping them zero in on the precise activities and experiences most essential to reaping gratitude’s benefits.

It has been revealed that it must be stated that actually capturing people in the moment of feeling gratitude poses some challenges. After all, some people may not feel gratitude when we expect them to, and others may even feel grateful in unexpected situations. I thought my best bet would be to try to induce gratitude through powerful stories of aid and sacrifice.

It has been revealed that to achieve this, I turned to the USC Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History, which houses the world’s largest repository of videotaped Holocaust survivor testimonies—many of which, perhaps surprisingly, are filled with breathtaking acts of selflessness and generosity. Along with a team of amazing undergraduates, I began by watching hundreds of hours of survivor testimony to find stories in which the survivor received help of some kind from another person.

Recent findings suggest that we assembled a collection of these stories and transformed them into short scenarios that we shared with our participants. Each scenario was re-phrased into the second-person (e.g., “You are on a wintertime death march and a fellow prisoner gives you a warm coat”) and presented to our study’s participants. We asked them to imagine themselves in the scenario and feel, as much as possible, how they would feel if they were in the same situation. While participants reflected on these gifts, we measured their brain activity using modern brain imaging techniques (in the form of functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI).

The regions associated with gratitude are part of the neural networks that light up when we socialize and experience pleasure.

For each of these scenarios, we asked participants how much gratitude they felt, and we correlated this rating with their brain activity in that moment. While such an approach will not elicit exactly the same feelings as actually living through such situations, participants overwhelmingly reported strong feelings of gratitude, deep engagement in the task, and, perhaps even more importantly, an increased empathy for and understanding of the Holocaust as a result of participating in the study.

What’s more, our results revealed that when participants reported those grateful feelings, their brains highlighted activity in a set of regions located in the medial pre-frontal cortex, an area in the frontal lobes of the brain where the two hemispheres meet. This area of the brain is associated with understanding other people’s perspectives, empathy, and feelings of relief. This is also an area of the brain that is massively connected to the systems in the body and brain that regulate emotion and support the process of stress relief.

These data told us a reasonable story about gratitude:.

Sources indicate that science suggests that expressing true gratitude boosts your health and spreads happiness. Here are a few simple exercises to help you build your capacity for gratitude. Read More ›.

In a recent development, gratitude isn’t just in our head: It takes root in our heart and in our senses, for one beautiful moment…and then the next. Here are three ways to practice gratitude, from a.m. to p.m. Read More ›.

Glenn Fox, PhD, is a research fellow at USC’s Brain and Creativity Institute. He earned his PhD from the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of Southern California working with Antonio Damasio. His research focuses on social cognition, affective neuroscience and social influence.

Founder Alex Crowder sought to move beyond the conventions of traditional floristry websites, creating instead a platform that could house her studio’s portfolio while articulating their deeper philosophy of working with nature rather than against it.

According to recent reports, drawing from historical horticultural publications, plant glossaries and garden almanacs, 1/1 Studio developed a design language that honours the depth of knowledge and integrity inherent in Field Studies Flora’s practice. The site functions as both a gallery of case studies and an educational resource, inviting visitors into a world where botanical understanding and artistic expression converge.

The visual identity and website design emphasise documentation and craft, mirroring the studio’s meticulous approach to their work. A film by Scott Macdonough, shot in the fields of Massachusetts, unveils the homepage, setting the tone for work born from connection to the natural world.

According to recent reports, the printed materials extend this language, creating a cohesive system that supports Field Studies Flora’s position at the intersection of horticulture, design and environmental stewardship. Typography and layout choices reference archival botanical texts, lending the contemporary practice a sense of scholarly rigor.

Industry News: ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali has formed a one-woman band.
  • It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
  • Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali has formed a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she notes. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Recent findings suggest that rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali notes. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

In a recent development, informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she indicates.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali claims. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

It has been revealed that as for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Recent findings suggest that shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

Recent findings suggest that A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

According to recent reports, I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

Industry observers note that november is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

Industry observers note that the culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the ‘turbulence and violence of our times’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
  • Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
  • According to recent reports, curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

According to recent reports, curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik states. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”.

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

Sources indicate that the Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik notes. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”.

These themes, Malik claims, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

Sources indicate that “I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik notes. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”.

It has been revealed that the Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

Recent findings suggest that the Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Recent findings suggest that finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

According to recent reports, “We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik indicates. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”.

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

How To Make Your Design System AI-Ready

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

According to recent reports, unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

It has been revealed that in fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

One of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

Sources indicate that to ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

According to recent reports, because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

Recent findings suggest that an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Sources indicate that ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

Recent findings suggest that the more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am presently VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

Sources indicate that we created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

In a recent development, next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

Industry observers note that after our pilot study with this newly introduced group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

Recent findings suggest that I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

It has been revealed that we ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

All participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as issues. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Industry observers note that issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an concern is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more complications and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

This site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall issues and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

Sources indicate that on this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more problems and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most complications.

Here, cognitive participants found 6 more problems and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

On this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more challenges and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

According to recent reports, something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more challenges on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

The other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more issues with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped concerns by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Industry observers note that let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability issues, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared issues and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more challenges related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

In a recent development, in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load issues consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

Sources indicate that these are improvements that would give all owners more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but vital issues with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

Anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout promptly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of owners, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

According to recent reports, these complications likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

According to recent reports, the study highlighted that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

According to recent reports, you create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability concerns start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some users.

Industry observers note that the percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

According to recent reports, people with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability issues that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology customers is still very important, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Sources indicate that cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

Sources indicate that in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more complications and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

Cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

This study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the matter and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

For this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with latest technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

It has been revealed that the boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

📅 2026-06-12 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

According to recent reports, I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

We have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

It has been revealed that the current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

What truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

In a recent development, yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

When this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

Industry observers note that if you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

Sources indicate that in the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

In a recent development, meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a company called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

While these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

In a recent development, they say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

In a recent development, outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

Sources indicate that in the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

According to recent reports, however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

On the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

According to recent reports, as humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

It has been revealed that the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very quickly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

In a recent development, there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

The dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

Recent findings suggest that if history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

The upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too big to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

It has been revealed that in the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

This shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

As the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” notes Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Recent findings suggest that reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Sources indicate that inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In a recent development, in the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

Industry observers note that the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into new objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” states Gianotten.

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

“We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving latest value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a fresh auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees).

  • It has been revealed that the 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a fresh auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.

Kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a newly introduced auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).

It has been revealed that no. 3P.B. (1960) by Yayoi Kusuma. Courtesy Sotheby's.

It has been revealed that the 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.

According to recent reports, roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.

Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.

One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.

Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.

The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.

Recent findings suggest that the top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.

Roy Lichtenstein's Two Paintings Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983) Courtesy Sotheby's.

In a recent development, it was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.

Recent findings suggest that not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.

After the sale, Sotheby’s remarked works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.

In a recent development, “When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, said following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—indicates it all.”.

On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

The mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

Sources indicate that the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

It has been revealed that spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

Recent findings suggest that the identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron notes the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert latest audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz states the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City.
  • Recent findings suggest that titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date.
  • It has been revealed that the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Recent findings suggest that titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

It has been revealed that the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

In a recent development, the installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a new location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

According to recent reports, for SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

The expansion also introduces more than 80 fresh retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

According to recent reports, yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

Recent findings suggest that the new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

#160427. Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

📅 2026-06-16 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3465 w)
📖 Baca
