Industry News: Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

📅 2026-07-02 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how users provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

To pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

According to recent reports, while they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our customers to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

The allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on customers. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

Industry observers note that when an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

Sources indicate that A blank chat box creates a major problem for users who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Industry observers note that designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

It has been revealed that having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

When an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status update. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

It has been revealed that the cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most notable.

Sources indicate that before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

According to recent reports, designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for users with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

In a recent development, table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

The following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

With this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

In a recent development, to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

According to recent reports, here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

Industry observers note that this is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because users often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

The Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

The Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-users and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

In a recent development, the Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

It has been revealed that once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

When you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your consumers.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

It has been revealed that with Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Consumers might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status patch only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

It has been revealed that table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve owners whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

In a recent development, field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

It has been revealed that to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

High-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

Second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

It has been revealed that the resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

In a recent development, the AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Sources indicate that once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

According to recent reports, an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

In a recent development, to get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

In a recent development, I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

We focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Recent findings suggest that use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • Industry observers note that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

Industry observers note that as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

In a recent development, we spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

One of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

Industry observers note that in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

Industry observers note that confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a massive believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

According to recent reports, clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

In a recent development, it got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to proposal? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

This sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

It has been revealed that kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

It has been revealed that my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

My conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

Recent findings suggest that we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Sources indicate that listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

Sources indicate that in my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, new perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

It has been revealed that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Big Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

In a recent development, an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Recent findings suggest that titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

Recent findings suggest that an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Sources indicate that the results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

Candelabra by Fort Standard, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

According to recent reports, participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Manufacturer, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. Individual contributors include Sophie Collé, Steven Bukowski, Kaye Blegvad, Hanna Anonen, and Fitzhugh Karol, bringing together practitioners working across furniture, objects, art, and other creative disciplines.

Recent findings suggest that candelabra by Hanna Anonen, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Click through the gallery above for a closer look at works featured in the exhibition.

Recent findings suggest that the exhibition also reflects Piscina’s broader interest in the intersection of art, design, and craft. Founded in 2013 by artist and furniture designer Natalie Shook as a cooperative studio, Piscina has since evolved into a gallery and showroom dedicated to contemporary collectible design. Earlier this year, it introduced a dedicated gallery space alongside a reimagined showroom, expanding its platform for independent artists and designers.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Timed to coincide with the season of gatherings and candlelit evenings, Candelabra Palaver offers a reminder that even the most familiar household objects can provide fertile ground for experimentation. Whether restrained or exuberant, functional or sculptural, each piece begins with the same basic premise and arrives somewhere different.

Candelabra Palaver is on view until Dec. 31, 2026, at Piscina in Brooklyn, Latest York. All works in the exhibition are available for purchase.

Candelabra by Dustin Barzell, featured in ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn. Photography courtesy of the artist and Piscina.

Users Don’t Need More Tools: They Need Seamless Integrations

📅 2026-07-03 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, we often hear about shiny upcoming tools that change everything (yet again).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, we often hear about shiny upcoming tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Owners don’t get excited about shiny fresh “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

Sources indicate that I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and big design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

It has been revealed that I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

Industry observers note that so no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, owners can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

Recent findings suggest that the instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

It has been revealed that it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where customers want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

User’s value doesn’t emerge from users having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping consumers do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

#160413. The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Design-milk ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack.
  • Of course, presentation matters, too.
  • Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Recent findings suggest that from Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

According to recent reports, from cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Sources indicate that porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

In a recent development, long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

According to recent reports, still shopping? Explore Design Milk’s Complete 2026 Holiday Gift Guide for more thoughtful finds for everyone on your list.

Photography courtesy of Maison Plage.

Sources indicate that for 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

Recent findings suggest that for a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

It has been revealed that food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

Not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Sources indicate that from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

According to recent reports, LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

From the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

Recent findings suggest that the most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

What does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Industry observers note that japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

Sources indicate that fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

According to recent reports, few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

In a recent development, from maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Industry observers note that art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

The Art Game Book is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

In a recent development, color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations. The 256-page hardcover is a colorful design object in its own right, with a seamless rainbow gradient wrapping around the cover and edges. It’s a joyful addition to any art lover’s collection.

Rainbow Dreams: Color and Light in Contemporary Art is available at phaidon.com for $40.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.

The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.

According to recent reports, grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.

According to recent reports, for Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.

Recent findings suggest that the Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and right now serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.

Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995–96) Photo: Nathan Keay, © MCA Chicago.

The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.

“In some cases, we are adding an entirely upcoming collection,” Grynsztejn states, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”.

The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.

During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.

Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she claims. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”.

Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings.
  • Davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain.
  • Recent findings suggest that established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation, Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” indicates Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

Schemata Architects Designs a Modern Chalet on Powder Mountain.

This year’s latest installations—from artists Jenny Holzer, Rose Wylie, and Xu Zhen—join an existing collection that includes works by Davina Semo, Nobuo Sekine, Nancy Holt, Kayode Ojo, and others. Each takes a different approach to interacting with the landscape. “I like having that range, rather than one consistent approach to what outdoor sculpture should look like,” Zhang notes.

Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026), featuring poetry by May Swenson carved into a native quartzite boulder, sits within the forested landscape of Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Whether skiing in winter or hiking and biking during warmer months, visitors may encounter THE EYE (2026), a upcoming installation by Jenny Holzer. The American neo-conceptual artist conceived of an evolving commission for Powder Mountain centered on work by the late Utah-born poet May Swenson.

Holzer selected a native quartzite boulder already embedded in the mountain, carving a phrase from Swenson’s poetry directly into the stone rather than relocating it or disturbing the surrounding vegetation: “The eye also a sun wanders and all that it sees it owns.”.

A close-up of Jenny Holzer’s ‘THE EYE’ (2026) reveals a line of poetry by May Swenson carved directly into a native quartzite boulder at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Blending into its natural surroundings, the work could easily go unnoticed by visitors who aren’t looking carefully. As snow, sunlight, and vegetation transform the landscape throughout the year, the inscription offers a point of continuity, even as the experience of encountering it changes.

THE EYE is the first in what Holzer looks to be an ongoing group of carved stones across the mountain. Like this one, future boulders will be selected on the mountain and the art created in place.

Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025), a 12-foot-tall painted bronze sculpture inspired by a pineapple she sketched in 2013, stands among towering pine trees at Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

It has been revealed that A decidedly different approach comes from Rose Wylie, whose Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb (2025) takes the form of a 12-foot-tall, bright pink painted bronze sculpture. The pineapple-like totem marks Wylie’s first permanent public sculpture in the U.S. The 92-year-old British painter describes the work as “poetic transformation,” which began in 2013 when she purchased a Ghanaian-grown pineapple at a local market. Struck by its distinctive surface and dramatic crown of leaves, she sketched the fruit.

A close-up of Rose Wylie’s ‘Pale-Pink Pineapple/Bomb’ (2025) highlights the exaggerated crown of leaves that gives the bright pink sculpture its distinctive silhouette. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Industry observers note that more than a decade later, those drawings have taken on a new dimension. Standing among 50-foot pine trees, the painted bronze sculpture retains the exaggerated silhouette of Wylie’s original sketches. Its form shifts between recognizable fruit, fantastical plant, and something more explosive, suggesting how scale and material can transform an ordinary subject into something entirely unexpected.

Recent findings suggest that unlike Holzer’s work, which is quite literally part of the scenery, Wylie’s is impossible to miss, its almost cartoonish silhouette creating an unexpected interruption in the natural landscape. Shanghai-based artist Xu Zhen takes yet another approach with Hello (2021–2022), which transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine form.

Xu Zhen’s ‘Hello’ (2021–2022) transforms a classical Corinthian column into a twisting, serpentine sculpture nestled among the aspen trees at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

In a recent development, to develop the sculpture’s serpentine form, Zhen studied the movements of snakes alongside representations of dragons and serpents from different cultures. He ultimately selected the Corinthian column for its ornate capital, whose leaf-like details suggested the head of a living creature. Using a 3D-scanned model as his starting point, he developed the form digitally before producing a full-scale prototype that informed the final bronze casting.

Sources indicate that “My work has always been about discovering alternative forms that an object might take,” the multimedia artist explains. “These forms should feel natural, as though the object was always meant to exist that way, while remaining outside our conventional understanding and experience.”.

Industry observers note that A close-up of Xu Zhen’s Hello (2021–2022) reveals the ornate Corinthian capital, whose leaf-like details give the twisting column an almost creature-like appearance. Photography by Kim Raff for Powder Art Foundation.

Installed among the mountain’s aspen trees, Hello takes on what Zhen describes as a “distinctly surreal quality.” Yet the setting also feels surprisingly natural. When he first saw the sculpture at Powder Mountain, the artist recalls feeling “that it had returned to the world where it belongs.”.

It has been revealed that for Zhang, the experience of encountering these works is as key as the artworks themselves. “You’re moving, your heart rate is up, there’s adrenaline, and then you come around a corner and encounter a work without expecting it,” he states. “I think being that engaged in your body changes how you experience the art.”.

It has been revealed that visitors to Powder Art Foundation’s fall open house gather around Nobuo Sekine’s Phase of Nothingness – Stone Stack (1970/2025) at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography by McCade Gordon for Powder Art Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that not every work is intended to have the same relationship to the mountain. “Some should feel like you discovered them; others should stop you in your tracks,” Zhang says. “The mountain connects everything.”.

Sources indicate that the Powder Mountain art trail opens for the winter season in mid-December, with lift-accessible installations available from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily and night access to the Sundown area from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. Access to the installations is included with a lift ticket or season pass.

According to recent reports, dalene Rovenstine is a New York–based writer and editor covering design, architecture, and lifestyle. She enjoys trying new restaurants, cheering on the Oklahoma City Thunder, and watching far too much TV. Her writing has appeared in Entertainment Weekly, TV Guide, Popular Mechanics, Hamptons, Luxe Interiors + Design, Interior Design, and more.

Fireclay Tile Turns Traditional Textiles Into Hand-Painted Tile

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces.
  • It has been revealed that interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all.
  • Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the latest hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

It has been revealed that interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”.

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

Industry observers note that that direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

Sources indicate that the Specimen Flowers series features four individual botanical motifs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—hand-painted on ceramic tile. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Specimen Flowers features four individual botanical designs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and Bluebell—that can be arranged across backsplashes, niches, and accent walls. The Idyllwild Florals take a more expansive approach, with repeating patterns named Pomegranate, Tulip, Morning Glory, and Meadow. Their overlapping stems, leaves, and blossoms create the dense, layered effect of a garden growing beyond its boundaries.

Sources indicate that the Stripes and Plaids explore a different kind of ornamentation. Four striped patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—introduce rhythm through repeated lines and geometric details. The Plaids, meanwhile, borrow the visual language of woven fabrics, with Chalet, Highlands, Minka, and Torp creating intersecting grids that can read as anything from understated texture to a bold, room-enveloping pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the Idyllwild Plaids series features four geometric patterns inspired by traditional woven textiles, shown here in warm shades of burgundy, pink, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

Sources indicate that while the designs reference traditional textiles, translating them into hand-painted ceramic required a different way of thinking about pattern. “We had to simplify and edit the artwork so our painting team could actually execute it by hand,” Jamie notes.

The process uses resist lines to define individual areas of color, making the scale and spacing of each detail particularly important. “When we translate intricate woven textiles into screen art, we have to pay very close attention to the thickness of the lines, how small the fields are to fill in, and making sure the painters have enough natural ‘starts and stops’ so they can work efficiently,” Jamie says.

A closer look at Fireclay Tile’s hand-painting process, with glaze applied to the Allium motif from the Idyllwild Specimen Flowers series. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

In a recent development, fireclay’s painting team was closely involved in prototyping, providing feedback on details that were too small or areas where the glaze couldn’t be applied smoothly. The company also developed a new glaze base specifically for the hand-application process.

The relationship between design and production extends to color. Each of the 16 patterns is available in four curated palettes inspired by the seasons, but developing those options required another significant undertaking.

The Meadow pattern from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild Florals series features an assortment of botanical motifs in the Spring color palette. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

In a recent development, fireclay’s previous hand-painted palette had become disconnected from its broader ceramic offering, limiting customization opportunities. To address that, the production team spent months matching the firm’s 50 core ceramic colors in both gloss and matte finishes. The resulting 100 finishes can be combined across the collection.

Recent findings suggest that A selection of floral, plaid, and striped patterns from Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection, shown in the Winter palette of deep blues, muted greens, and warm neutrals. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

To develop Idyllwild’s seasonal palettes, the team worked with physical tile samples alongside 4K renderings, testing combinations before translating them into paint sheets for production. The color stories also reflect shifts the company has been observing in interiors, including an interest in deeper reds and earthy blues.

2027 Colors of the Year: The Shades Defining Design.

“Organizing the collection into four seasonal motifs really shows how much color shifts the personality of a design: a plaid in soft pastels feels light and cottage-like, whereas that same pattern in deep, moody tones reads like a cozy wool blanket,” Jamie explains.

Industry observers note that the Idyllwild Stripes series features four hand-painted patterns—Stuga, Mokki, Blockhaus, and Thatch—combining linear details and geometric motifs in shades of blue, green, and brown. Photography courtesy of Fireclay Tile.

The collection also introduces new sizes, including 2-by-8-inch and 3-by-6-inch tiles, designed to work alongside standard field tiles. This allows patterns to be introduced selectively or carried across larger surfaces, with stripes used as borders or accents and more intricate designs covering entire walls.

Although Idyllwild draws from traditional patterns, the finished designs are shaped as much by the practical demands of hand-painting as by their textile references.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.
  • The whole system starts with a single chevron.
  • The custom typeface carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

The whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking new ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it shows in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

In a recent development, one frame shows the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the organization actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

#160407. Breaking: Designing For Distressed Consumers: Why Mental Health Apps Shouldn’t Follow Every UI Fashion
