#160309. Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Upcoming York

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1665 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Upcoming York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Newly introduced York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Industry observers note that still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a upcoming home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of important 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Industry observers note that illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

According to recent reports, gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Fresh York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

It has been revealed that gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Fresh York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a newly introduced auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Industry observers note that the appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Upcoming York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

In a recent development, large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Recent findings suggest that measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and crucial champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Latest York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Industry observers note that apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca remarked. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

#160307. SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing fresh life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.
  • The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns.
  • The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing fresh life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing upcoming life into this beloved building,” remarked SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

Recent findings suggest that it is part of a wider renovation SOM unveiled for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these latest structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” stated SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”.

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in Upcoming York in 2021, with prepares for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson.

Perron shapes Quebec kitchen around tea collection

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.
  • Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.
  • Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Paul Dussault.

A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” mentioned Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most vital to her.”.

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” stated Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” stated the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Made Thought builds the Juana brand identity on acid lime and amber, a CBD skincare system where dense label type meets macro botanical light.

It has been revealed that juana is a CBD-powered skincare brand, and Made Thought frames it as half family tradition, half skincare innovation. Founder Yann Moujawaz comes from a line of surgeons and Syrian olive grove stewards, and his formulations aim to switch on the skin's own renewal with expert precision. The design answers a market full of noise and false claims with something that looks like proof: warm amber glass, clinical label density, and botanical photography shot like evidence. The palette does the arguing. Acid lime cuts against deep olive and burnt orange, and the amber packs glow against it all like samples held up to the light.

The wordmark is a compact grotesque JUANA in capitals, set small and quiet on every pack, letting the label copy do the talking. On the lime tubes, ingredient lists run down the barrel in tight bilingual columns, English beside French, with the CBD strength called out large: 100mg on the cleanser, 300mg on the face cream, plus vitamin E, jojoba oil, and hyaluronic acid in the same breath.

Recent findings suggest that at poster scale the same type goes loud. Nurture Facial Cleanser, 100mg CBD fills the frame in acid lime, underlined, with the pack leaning into the shot. The web panel pairs a flat lime block reading Full Spectrum Cannabinoids with a hand dipping into a jar, and a line-drawn diagram of the whole range sits on olive like a spec sheet. The system holds together because the grid never changes, only the scale does.

The materials carry the science half of the story. Amber glass keeps the formulas away from the light, frosted lime plastic softens the tubes, and matte black caps close every silhouette. White outer cartons stack in a stepped row with a single lime band along the top edge, the only colour the box allows itself. Macro shots push closer still: a pipette suspended in fortifying face oil, bubbles rising through amber, and a leaf photographed so tight its veins turn into a map of yellow, green, and blue.

It has been revealed that founder Yann Moujawaz calls the partnership magic, saying passion was generously poured into it, and the photography backs him up. Nothing here is styled to look expensive for its own sake. The glow comes from the product itself, amber oil against orange light, and the identity lets it show.

See more from Made Thought on their website.

#160299. Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (699 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

Sources indicate that this eventually led to the fresh, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

It has been revealed that the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Industry observers note that objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

According to recent reports, the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a latest model of partnership”.

This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

It has been revealed that the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

Sources indicate that the earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

Recent findings suggest that the three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a upcoming display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

#160292. Latest Update: Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • In a recent development, before the auction, Sotheby’s had not declared a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the Newly introduced York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

In a recent development, before the auction, Sotheby’s had not declared a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

Industry observers note that urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

It has been revealed that comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

Sources indicate that then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Industry observers note that following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a upcoming owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

It has been revealed that the terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to Upcoming York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

In a recent development, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

#160291. “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1526 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

“We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its blueprint to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Unveiled by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with fresh housing by 2051.
  • Recent findings suggest that officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its blueprint to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Unveiled by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with fresh housing by 2051.

Recent findings suggest that officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political glitch in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” remarked Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are at the moment not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

Newly introduced facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Recent findings suggest that energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

Industry observers note that the matter is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are presently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Problems Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

Recent findings suggest that the team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.

Recent findings suggest that “It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the problem.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

In a recent development, “The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

It has been revealed that “We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the substantial-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” remarked Robinson.

Industry observers note that “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.
  • Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.

“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”.

The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” mentioned Zimbalist.

“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”.

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.

“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

“‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”.

Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”.

Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.

As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.

Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.

Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world?
  • Sources indicate that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • In a recent development, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

Sources indicate that while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report claims.

In a recent development, the data also indicates that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report states. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents noted they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also revealed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

It has been revealed that the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among fresh collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

According to recent reports, but can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

It has been revealed that the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report indicates. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

It has been revealed that “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

  • On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).

Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and reveals how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.

On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.

The dioramas – a Ferris wheel, rollercoaster, helter-skelter, dodgems and carousel – resemble some of Suzuki‘s earlier work, such as the interactive Sonic Bloom installation in London.

“The ideas have existed in my sketchbooks for the last couple of years and have gradually developed through a series of my public art projects,” Suzuki told Dezeen.

“I’ve always been interested in expanding the scale of my sound sculptures, imagining how they might eventually become architectural structures or even full-scale amusement park rides.”.

The designer 3D-printed the kinetic sculptures, which move and are accompanied by their own soundtracks, from polylactic acid (PLA) plastic.

“The dioramas are mainly made using 3D-printed materials, alongside modified HO-scale miniature structures,” he said.

“I had picked up traditional amusement park components – roller coaster, ferris wheel, helter-skelter, carousel, and dodge cars – to visualise my ideas for sound sculptures and architectural structures that could potentially be realised on a larger scale in the future.”.

Suzuki has been drawn to amusement parks all his life, and with Onomatopia he wanted to explore how they could help create a utopian city.

“I’ve been fascinated by theme parks since I was a child, particularly Disneyland, but also the relationship between amusement parks, world expos and urban planning, from Coney Island as explored in Rem Koolhaas’s Delirious New York to the 1889 Paris Exposition,” he explained.

“I had the opportunity to work with Disney Imagineering, who create Disney parks, and I became particularly interested in Walt Disney’s original vision for EPCOT (Experimental Prototype of Community of Tomorrow),” Suzuki continued.

“It imagined an ideal city rather than simply a theme park, and Onomatopia is my own attempt to imagine a utopian city shaped by sound, drawing on my experience creating public installations.”.

Suzuki, who is known for his sound design, has previously created pieces such as an acoustic playground in Shanghai and a “trumpet-like” San Francisco art installation.

“For me, theme parks and expos are fascinating because they bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience within an imagined world, almost like an experiment in creating a utopian city,” Suzuki explained.

The designer drew on his experience of working on a large-scale sound design when creating these smaller versions of his sculptures.

“Over the last couple of years I have been involved in some large city development projects, such as creating Metropolis Symphony for One Bangkok and my initial involvement in planning around the V&A East (East Bank) development,” Suzuki noted.

“I’ve become increasingly interested in how sound can shape public spaces, and my own idea of utopia is a place where sound contributes to wellbeing and encourages communication between people, beyond the boundaries of language and culture.”.

It has been revealed that onomatopia is on show at Osh Gallery, The Old Sorting House, 46 Essex Road, London from 10 November 2026 to 7 January 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Sources indicate that A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

The critical distinction is probate. In states with expensive or slow probate processes — California, Fresh York, Florida, and many others — a living trust pays for itself many times over. In states with simplified probate procedures (like Texas or Wisconsin for small estates), the cost advantage of a trust is smaller but the privacy and incapacity benefits still apply.

According to recent reports, you need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

According to recent reports, the term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

It has been revealed that an irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:.

In a recent development, the federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

According to recent reports, for most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

In a recent development, nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate proposal.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:.

A will alone is likely sufficient if:.

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:.

Add irrevocable trust structures if:.

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

In a recent development, the most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate strategy.

Industry observers note that yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

In a recent development, A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific challenges or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

Sources indicate that A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Sources indicate that without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

Sources indicate that the living trust vs will decision is not about which is better — it is about which is better for your specific situation. For estates with more than $100,000 in probatable assets, especially in high-cost probate states, a revocable living trust saves thousands of dollars and months of delay while providing incapacity protection and privacy that a will cannot match. For smaller estates in simplified-probate states, a well-drafted will with proper beneficiary designations may be all you need. Either way, the worst estate initiative is no estate plan. More than 60% of American adults have neither a will nor a trust, leaving their families to navigate probate without guidance, pay avoidable costs, and endure unnecessary delays during the most difficult time of their lives.

Recent findings suggest that the Black and White Photo Awards 2026 winners have been unveiled. Photographers competed across six categories, each vying to be named Black and White Photographer of the Year.

Speaking of which, this year’s big winner is Shengwei Dai, who took the top spot for a spectacular shot of a man jumping between two moving trains, with dozens of passengers looking on.

Dai earned a €1,500 cash prize for the win, the largest single award in the competition’s five-year history.

Alongside Dai’s overall win, competition judges selected winners across six categories: Architecture, Fauna and Flora, Landscape, Portrait, Street, and the new Open Theme.

“The fresh category aims to welcome photographs that, through their artistic, narrative, or conceptual approach, do not fit neatly into any of the traditional disciplines,” the Black and White Photo Awards explains.

Each category also includes Golden, Silver, and Bronze mentions, which serve as runner-up and honorable mention distinctions. Category winners each receive a €200 cash prize.

Photographer Qian Shen won the Architecture category with a striking shot of the Suzhou Olympic Sports Center in China.

Industry observers note that mohammad Mirza’s photo, Silent Majesty, earned the top spot in the Fauna and Flora category. The image captures a white rhinoceros emerging through the mist and trees in Kenya’s Solio Reserve, a private wildlife sanctuary.

Jie Fischer’s Flamingo in Flight 2 bested the competition in the Landscape category. The nearly abstract aerial shot captures a flock of flying flamingos from a top-down perspective against a high-contrast, pattern-filled terrain.

Happy Mukherjee’s portrait, Behind the Silence, depicts a young girl and invites viewers to wonder about her expression and gaze.

Cow Watching by Chongfeng Wu won the Street category. Unlike most street photos captured in urban environments, Wu’s pastoral shot is much quieter.

The inaugural Open Theme winner is Lloyd Lane, whose image, Convergence, captures a flock of starlings over Brighton Palace Pier in England.

The judges also selected finalists across all six categories, and their work can be viewed on the Black and White Photo Awards website.

The Black and White Photo Awards is already looking forward to its sixth annual competition in 2027, with entries opening on January 1.
